title.narrative: Disaster Risk Management Development Policy Credit with a Catastrophe Deferred Drawdown Option (Cat DDO)

description.narrative: The Disaster Risk Management (DRM) Development Policy Financing with a Catastrophe Deferred Drawdown Option (DPF with Cat DDO), in the amount of Euro 165.4 million (US$200 million equivalent), will support the Government of Kenya's (GoK) reform program to improve the country's capacity to reduce disaster risks and improve management of the socioeconomic and fiscal impacts of disasters. The GoK has initiated a shift toward a more proactive approach to managing disaster and climate risks. This has involved taking systematic steps to develop a comprehensive approach to overall risk management, including addressing impacts of climate change (CC), to build programs and strategies that strengthen national response, and put in place contingency financing that will serve to improve post-disaster liquidity needed to meet emergency and recovery needs. Under the devolved governance structure that was established by the Constitution of Kenya 2010, the country's forty-seven county governments play a key role in DRM1. The Constitution integrates key provisions on DRM including national level support to counties which are required to develop their respective DRM policies and programs in line with the National DRM Policy. Extreme climatic events have long posed a significant risk to Kenya, and contributed to increasing levels of vulnerability of the poor, smallholder farmers and pastoralists, whose livelihoods are threatened by increased variability of rainfall patterns, triggering episodes of acute food insecurity. Kenya is at an early stage of urbanization, but by 2050 about half of the population will be living in cities. Around 27 percent of Kenyans live in urban areas, and the country is urbanizing at about 4.3 percent a year. The urbanization process has been accompanied by increasing levels of urban poverty (60 percent of Kenya's urban households live in slums), growth of informal settlements, poorly functioning land markets and institutions, and an incomplete legal and building regulatory framework. Historical factors underpinning land ownership have led to urban land market distortions and, today, these markets are having difficulty supporting sustainable urbanization. In addition, there is low technical capacity to enforce and to build resilient infrastructure, making the country and its population particularly vulnerable. Evidence of this is the proliferation of substandard buildings with poor services and insufficient infrastructure, with the collapse of more than 26 buildings in the last 20 years. Equally important is the exposure of urban areas to moderate seismic risk, due to the East African Rift running through west Kenya and fault lines that are present south of Mombasa.
The overall PDO is to strengthen the Government of Kenya's institutional, technical, and financial capacities to manage the impact of climate and disaster risks.

comment.narrative:
<p>As of August 2022, the draft Handbook was developed and national consultations are ongoing.</p>

<p> </p>

<p>This RI was partially achieved. </p>

title.narrative: Urban resilience strategies prepared to enhance city management

comment.narrative:
<p>The procurement process for a firm to develop urban resilience strategies in five cities (Nairobi, Mombasa, Kisumu, Eldoret and Nakuru), under the WB Kenya Urban Support Programme, experienced significant delays, which impacted this indicator. A firm was eventually contracted in September 2021 and the urban resilience strategies are expected to be developed by April 2023. </p>

<p> </p>

<p>This RI was not achieved.</p>

title.narrative: County level emergency and/or contingency plans adopted that strengthens response capacity

comment.narrative:
<p>As of August 2022, 8 County Emergency Operations Plans (CEOPs) have been developed from the National Emergency Response Plan andsubsequent guidance note.</p>

<p> - 6 CEOPs were adopted with evidence provided for 3 (Lamu, Kisumu, Muranga) and waiting for evidence for 3 (Kakamega, Turkana and Isiolo)</p>

<p> - 2 CEOPs are pending approval for Nairobi and Wajir.</p>

<p>???????</p>

<p>This RI was substantially achieved.</p>

title.narrative: Reports on consolidated postdisaster expenditure produced annually and submitted to the Budget Department within National Treasury

comment.narrative:
<p>The NT team submitted a total of five reports covering: (i) locust infestation in FY 19/20, (ii) floods in FY19/20, (iii) droughts in FY 19/20, (iv) other minor disasters in FY 19/20 and (v) COVID-19 epidemic in FY 19/20. The NT acknowledges that the RI requires three reports produced annually, however, due to the time required to set up the reporting infrastructure and the time it currently takes to collect and process data, reports for the FY 18/19 were not produced and reports for the FY 20/21 are not yet available.</p>

<p> </p>

<p>This RI was achieved.</p>

title.narrative: Number of households eligible for disaster relief through financial protection instruments

comment.narrative:
<p>There are four programs whose beneficiaries are tracked towards achievement of RI 9: (i) the KAIP; (ii) the KLIP; (iii) the HSNP; and (iv) the Food Systems Project jointly implemented by the NDMA and WFP. </p>

<p>During 2018/19 and 2019/20 the number of eligible households was above the target (almost double the target in 2019/20). However, due to budget cuts to the droughtprograms driven by COVID-19 related demands, this number has been decreasing. In 2020/2021 this number fell to 160,962 and it fell further in 2021/22 to 65,000 households.</p>

<p>This RI is partially achieved. For 2 of the 3 years of the Operation it was achieved, but not the final year.</p>

title.narrative: National Disaster Risk Management Strategy that strengthens government coordination for climate resilience and DRM adopted

comment.narrative:
<p>A draft DRM Strategy has been developed, but as of August 2022, it has not be finalized or approved.</p>
<p> This RI was partially achieved.</p>

title.narrative: Establishment of a national climate finance mechanism to support mobilization, coordination and tracking of climate finance from both internal and external sources

comment.narrative:
<p>The National climate finance mechanism which is the combination of the establishment of a national climate finance fund and the development climate finance tracking system.</p>

<p> - The regulations to create the <strong>national climate finance fund </strong>were developed are not yet endorsed by the Ministry of Environment and Forestry (MoEF) and thus the fund is not operational.</p>

<p> - The <strong>climate finance tracking system</strong> was developed and used to mainstream climate finance across government and integrate it within the National Treasury's accounting system. </p>

<p> </p>

<p>This RI is partially achieved.</p>

title.narrative: National Water Harvesting and Storage Authority established for improved water resource and drought management

comment.narrative:
<p>Progress made following the establishment of the National Water Harvesting and Storage Authority (NWHSA) includes: (i) the Authority has developed a 5-year strategic plan that covers the period 2018-2022; (ii) the management structure is being finalized, and (iii) NWHSA is working towards establishing five regional offices across the Country.</p>

<p> </p>

<p>This RI was achieved.</p>
